cards.front: What does it mean for two events to be [[kw:disjoint]]?
cards.back: They have no outcomes in common. Also called [[imp:mutually exclusive]]. Example: rolling a die and getting an even number or a number greater than 6. Their Venn diagram circles do not overlap.
Events that share at least one outcome. Their Venn diagram circles intersect. Example: drawing a face card or a spade from a deck.

cards.front: Define the [[kw:union]] of two events $A$ and $B$.
cards.back: The set of all outcomes that are in $A$, in $B$, or in both. Written as $A \cup B$, it corresponds to "$A$ or $B$".
The set of all outcomes that are in both $A$ and $B$. Written as $A \cap B$, it corresponds to "$A$ and $B$".
cards.front: Define the [[kw:intersection]] of two events $A$ and $B$.
What is the addition rule for [[kw:disjoint events]]?
cards.back: $$ P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) $$ Because the events have no overlap, you simply add their probabilities.

cards.front: What is the general addition rule for [[kw:overlapping events]]?
cards.back: $$ P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B) $$ This prevents double‑counting the intersection.

cards.front: Why do we subtract $P(A \text{ and } B)$ in the general addition rule?
cards.back: When we add $P(A)$ and $P(B)$, the outcomes in the intersection are counted twice. Subtracting $P(A \text{ and } B)$ once corrects the overcount.

cards.front: A card is drawn from a 52‑card deck. Find $P(10 \text{ or face card})$.
A card is drawn from a 52‑card deck. Find $P(\text{face card or spade})$.
How can you find $P(A \text{ and } B)$ if you know $P(A)$, $P(B)$, and $P(A \text{ or } B)$?
cards.back: Rearrange the general addition rule: $$ P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ or } B) $$
To organize sequences of events, showing probabilities on branches. Multiply along a branch for "and", then add branches for "or" to find total probability of an event.
cards.front: What is a [[kw:probability tree diagram]] used for?
State the [[kw:Law of Total Probability]] for two complementary conditions $A$ and $\overline{A}$.
cards.back: If event $B$ can occur either with $A$ or with its complement $\overline{A}$: $$ P(B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A) + P(\overline{A}) \cdot P(B \mid \overline{A}) $$
Use Law of Total Probability: $$ P(\text{correct}) = 0.083 \times 0.98 + 0.917 \times 0.95 = 0.08134 + 0.87115 = 0.95249 $$ About 95.2%.
cards.front: A medical test is 98% accurate for those with a disease (8.3% have it), and 95% for those without. Find $P(\text{correct diagnosis})$.

cards.back: $$ P(\overline{A}) = 1 - P(A) $$ All probabilities in a sample space add to 1.
